190.title: Thou hast searched me (Psalm 138 [139])
190.hook: you knit me in my mother's womb, and there's nowhere God is not
190.tomorrow: let every spirit praise the Lord
190.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 138 [139] in the Liturgy of the Hours, and a verse of it shapes the traditional entrance chant of Easter Sunday; some pray its closing lines before an examination of conscience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, by the rivers of Babylon, remembering Sion: exiles weeping, and rage handed to God. Your line was even anger can be prayed. Did you try it? Today, a psalm about being seen all the way through. Day one hundred ninety.

Some rooms in a life stay locked. A thing done at nineteen. A thought never said out loud. The self that shows up at two in the morning. People let each other into the front hallway and keep the rest shut. Being fully known can be frightening. Never being known at all can be lonely. Today's psalm stands right between those two. It says: you have been seen in every room, and you have not been walked out on. Today: thou hast searched me.
screen: `A FEW LOCKED ROOMS.` → `AFRAID OF BEING KNOWN.` → `LONELY IF WE'RE NOT.`

segments.voice: The title is the older English wording: thou hast searched me. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, says: "Lord, thou hast proved me, and known me." Proved, as in tested. Under both is the Hebrew chaqar, to search out, to examine through and through. First, known. The psalmist says God knows his sitting down and his rising up, understands his thoughts from far off, knows his ways before he takes them. That could sound like surveillance. It doesn't read like that. It reads like wonder. Second, nowhere God is not. In the Douay-Rheims: "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy face? If I ascend into heaven, thou art there: if I descend into hell, thou art present." Up, down, the far end of the sea, the dark itself: the psalmist tries every exit and finds God already there, not to trap him, but to hold him. Even darkness, he says, is not dark to you. Third, made. "Thou hast protected me from my mother's womb," the Douay says, and the psalmist marvels at how he was formed before anyone saw him. Before anyone else knew he existed, he was known. Catholics hear this psalm at Easter: the old entrance chant of Easter Sunday, Resurrexi, draws on a verse of it, I arose, and am still with thee. And the psalm ends where it started, but now as a request: prove me, O God, and know my heart. The same knowing that could have been frightening becomes something he asks for.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in being fully known. Settle, and breathe. If there's a locked room in your own life, let yourself remember it's there. You don't have to open it or name it out loud. Then, if you pray, rest in the psalm's claim that God has already seen that room and hasn't left. You can say its closing words: prove me, O God, and know my heart. If you don't pray, simply breathe, and let yourself be all of who you are for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Chaqar. Hebrew to search out, examine through, the root behind thou hast searched me, the psalm about being known completely, everywhere, and still held. Today's word.
Your line: known, and not left. Today, let one person see a little more of you than usual, or be someone who stays when you see more of them. Day one hundred ninety.

191.title: Let every spirit praise the Lord (Psalm 150)
191.hook: trumpets, harp, timbrel, cymbals, and everything that breathes
191.howItsDone: Catholics sing the Alleluia before the Gospel at Mass, omit it through Lent, and bring it back at the Easter Vigil; Psalm 150 is prayed at Morning Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, thou hast searched me, chaqar: seen in every room, and still held. Your line was known, and not left. Who stayed? Today, the last psalm of all. Day one hundred ninety-one.

Trumpet. Psaltery and harp. Timbrel and choir. Strings and organs. High-sounding cymbals, then cymbals of joy. That's the last psalm in the book, and it reads like a finale, every player coming in at once and nobody holding anything back for later. The book of Psalms carries joy and grief, anger and trust. It ends here: every instrument sounding, and then the music handed to anyone with breath in their lungs. Today's word is the one it's built on: Alleluia.
screen: `THE LAST PSALM: A FINALE.` → `EVERY INSTRUMENT AT ONCE.` → `THEN, EVERYONE WHO BREATHES.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Alleluia is Hebrew, hallelu-Yah: hallelu, all of you, praise, and Yah, a short form of God's name. So it isn't a feeling, it's an invitation: everybody, praise God. It came into Greek and Latin untranslated, and Catholics still sing it that way today. Second, the orchestra. Psalm 150 is six verses and almost every line is a call to praise. It moves out from the sanctuary to the sky, then through the band. In the Douay-Rheims: "Praise him with sound of trumpet: praise him with psaltery and harp." Then timbrel and choir, strings and organs, and two kinds of cymbals. Nothing is held back. Third, the last line. After all the instruments, it lands on the one instrument everybody has. "Let every spirit praise the Lord. Alleluia." The Hebrew says everything that has breath. The Latin, and the Douay after it, say spirit. You don't need a trumpet. You need lungs. Fourth, how Catholics keep this word. The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel at Mass. But through the whole of Lent, the Church goes without it. On Easter night, at the Vigil, it comes back, sung three times, rising each time. So this is the end of our Psalms. Over thirty-five days we walked from the two ways of Psalm one, through the shepherd, the Miserere, the pilgrims' road, the depths and the rivers of exile, to a finale where everything that breathes is invited to join.
screen: `HALLELU-YAH: EVERYBODY, PRAISE GOD.` · `TRUMPET, HARP, TIMBREL, CYMBALS.` · `THE LAST INSTRUMENT: BREATH.` · `SILENT IN LENT, BACK AT EASTER.` · then, large: `LET EVERY SPIRIT PRAISE THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a slow alleluia. Settle, and breathe. Notice your breath going in and out on its own, without you asking. Now, on one long out-breath, let the word ride out quietly: al-le-lu-ia. Then just breathe for a while, and do it again when you're ready. If you pray, it's praise. If you don't, it's simply a long, slow breath out, noticing that you're alive. The bell holds the time.
Alleluia. From the Hebrew hallelu-Yah: all of you, praise God. The word the Psalms end on. Today's word.

Your line: everything that breathes. Today, notice one living thing breathing, a dog asleep, a baby, a bird, the person next to you, and count it in the choir. Tomorrow we open a gospel and read it straight through. Day one hundred ninety-one.

192.title: The beginning (Mark 1:1–8)
192.hook: no birth story, just the beginning of the good news and a voice in the desert
192.howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics stand for the Gospel, trace a small cross on forehead, lips and heart as it is announced, and hear it read by a deacon or priest; the Gospel of Mark is read on most Sundays in Year B of the lectionary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Alleluia, and the Psalms ended with everything that breathes. That was your line. Did you count someone into the choir? Today we open a new book, and read it straight through. Day one hundred ninety-two.

Most stories about a famous person start with a birth. A baby, a family, a hometown, a childhood. Matthew and Luke do that: angels, shepherds, wise men, a stable. Mark doesn't. No manger. No star. No Mary and Joseph on the road. Mark opens with one line, like a title card at the start of a film, and then drops you straight into the desert, where a wild man in camel's hair is shouting at crowds. For the next forty days we'll read Mark from start to finish, a few verses at a time. Today's word is the one in his first sentence: gospel.
screen: `NO MANGER. NO STAR.` → `ONE LINE, LIKE A TITLE CARD.` → `FORTY DAYS OF MARK.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In the Douay-Rheims: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." That's the whole first verse. Mark tells you what he's writing and who it's about, and doesn't waste a word. Second, the word. Gospel comes from old English, god-spel, good story, good news. Mark wrote in Greek, and his word is euangelion. In his world it was the word for big public news: a victory announced, a new emperor, a royal birth, sent out by messengers to every town. Greek Isaiah used the same root for heralds running ahead of God, and Paul was already using the word for the message about Jesus. Mark sets it over the whole story. This, he says, is the real headline. Third, the voice. Mark quotes the prophets: "A voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight his paths." And there's John the Baptist, living rough, dressed in camel's hair with a leather belt, eating locusts and wild honey, calling people to be baptized in the Jordan and to turn their lives around. Crowds come out from the whole countryside and from Jerusalem. And then John points away from himself. Someone mightier is coming after me, he says; I'm not worthy to stoop down and untie his sandals. Fourth, the book. Mark is the shortest of the four gospels. Many scholars think it was the first written, and an early tradition says Mark set down what he'd heard Peter preach. You can read it aloud in about two hours. It moves fast. We'll feel that tomorrow.
screen: `THE BEGINNING OF THE GOSPEL.` · `EUANGELION: PUBLIC GOOD NEWS.` · `A VOICE CRYING IN THE DESERT.` · `THE SHORTEST GOSPEL, AND FAST.` · then, large: `PREPARE YE THE WAY OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the first line aloud. Settle, and breathe. If you have a Bible or your phone nearby, find Mark chapter one, verse one. If not, use the words you heard: the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Say it out loud, slowly, the way a herald would announce news in a town square. Then sit with it. What would good news sound like, for you, today? If you pray, you can offer that. The bell holds the time.
Gospel. Old English for good news, from the Greek euangelion, the word for news big enough to send heralds. Today's word.
Your line: gospel means good news. Today, be the one who carries good news to someone: a thank-you, a well done, a thing that went right. Day one hundred ninety-two.

193.title: Straight into the desert (Mark 1:9–13)
193.hook: baptism, the voice, then the Spirit drives him out among the wild beasts
193.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Baptism of the Lord as the feast that closes the Christmas season, and hear Mark's short account of the forty days in the desert on the First Sunday of Lent in Year B.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beginning of Mark, and the word gospel. Your line was gospel means good news. Whose good news did you carry? Today, Jesus walks into the story. Day one hundred ninety-three.

Some storytellers linger. They give you the weather, the smell of the kitchen, what everyone was wearing. Mark is not one of them. Mark is the friend who tells a story so fast you have to say, wait, back up. In five verses today, Jesus arrives from a small village, is baptized in a river, sees the sky rip open, hears a voice, and is driven out into the wilderness for forty days. Five verses. Mark has a favorite word for this speed, and you're going to start hearing it everywhere. Today: straight into the desert.
screen: `SOME STORYTELLERS LINGER.` → `MARK DOES NOT.` → `FIVE VERSES, FORTY DAYS.`

segments.voice: First, the river. Jesus comes from Nazareth in Galilee, and John baptizes him in the Jordan. Mark doesn't stop to explain why. He just moves. Second, the word. In the Douay-Rheims: "And forthwith coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens opened, and the Spirit as a dove descending, and remaining on him." Forthwith. Older English Bibles say straightway. In Greek it's euthys, immediately, right then. Mark reaches for it again and again. Watch for it. It gives his whole gospel the feeling of running. Third, the sky. Where the English says opened, Mark's Greek actually says the heavens were torn, ripped like cloth. And a voice from heaven says: you are my beloved Son, in you I am well pleased. Catholics see the whole Trinity in this moment: the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, the Father's voice. Fourth, the desert. And then, immediately again. In the Douay-Rheims: "And immediately the Spirit drove him out into the desert." Drove is a strong word, the same word Mark later uses for driving out demons. Jesus is there forty days, tempted by Satan, with the wild beasts, and angels serve him. That's it. Mark gives one sentence. He doesn't tell us what the temptations were; Matthew and Luke do that. Mark leaves the temptations untold, and adds a detail of his own: the wild beasts. Beloved, and straight into the wilderness: in Mark, being loved by God doesn't mean an easy road. It means the road starts right away.
screen: `FROM NAZARETH TO THE JORDAN.` · `EUTHYS: STRAIGHTWAY.` · `THE HEAVENS TORN OPEN.` · `DRIVEN INTO THE WILDERNESS.` · then, large: `THE SPIRIT DROVE HIM OUT INTO THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice how fast Mark moves, and how fast you do. Settle, and breathe. Replay your morning in your head, quickly: woke up, and straightway, phone. And straightway, coffee. And straightway, the next thing. Notice how few pauses there were. Now, for these two minutes, don't go straightway anywhere. Stay put. If you pray, you can rest in the words spoken over Jesus at the river: beloved. If you don't, just rest. The bell holds the time.
Euthys. Mark's favorite Greek word, straightway, immediately, carrying Jesus from the river to the wilderness in a single breath, his baptism and his forty days. Today's word.
Your line: straightway. Today, every time you hear yourself rushing, say the word in your head, and see if one thing can wait a breath. Day one hundred ninety-three.

194.title: Fishers of men (Mark 1:14–20)
194.hook: the kingdom is at hand, and fishermen leave their nets
194.howItsDone: Catholics hear the call of the first disciples at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and the pope wears the Ring of the Fisherman as a sign of succession to Saint Peter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, straight into the desert, euthys: the river, the torn sky, the forty days. Your line was straightway. Did anything wait a breath? Today, the first followers. Day one hundred ninety-four.

A lake in Galilee. Two brothers stand in the shallows, throwing a round net out over the water, hauling it in, throwing it again. Down the shore, two more brothers sit in their father's boat, mending nets. Ordinary work, done with the hands, the same today as yesterday. Then a man walks along the beach, stops, and calls to them. Before long, all four have left that shore. Today: fishers of men.
screen: `A LAKE IN GALILEE.` → `CASTING NETS, MENDING NETS.` → `A MAN WALKS ALONG THE SHORE.`

segments.voice: First, the announcement. John the Baptist has been arrested, and Jesus comes into Galilee with a message you can say in one breath. In the Douay-Rheims: "The time is accomplished, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent, and believe the gospel." At hand means close enough to touch. Repent, in Greek metanoia, means more than feeling sorry. It means turning your mind around, facing a new way. Second, the call. Jesus sees Simon and his brother Andrew casting their nets into the sea, and says: "Come after me, and I will make you to become fishers of men." He uses their own work. You catch fish; now you'll gather people. Third, the leaving. And, Mark's favorite word again: "And immediately leaving their nets, they followed him." A little further on he calls James and John, the sons of Zebedee, and they leave their father in the boat with the hired men and go. Notice what Mark doesn't say. He doesn't say whether they'd heard Jesus preach before. He doesn't say what they felt, or what their father said. John's gospel suggests some of them had met Jesus earlier; Mark just shows the leaving. Fourth, why Catholics care. Simon is the one Jesus will call Peter, and Catholics see in him the first of the popes. A pope receives a ring called the Ring of the Fisherman, a reminder of a beach and men who dropped their nets.
screen: `THE KINGDOM IS AT HAND.` · `COME AFTER ME.` · `THEY LEFT THEIR NETS AND FATHER.` · `THE RING OF THE FISHERMAN.` · then, large: `I WILL MAKE YOU TO BECOME FISHERS OF MEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the work in your hands. Settle, and breathe. Jesus called the fishermen through the work they already knew. Think of the ordinary work your hands will do today: a keyboard, a steering wheel, a sink of dishes, a child's shoelaces. Name it plainly. Now let your hands rest, still, for these two minutes. If you pray, you can offer that ordinary work to God, nets and all. If you don't, just notice what your hands do all day, and let them rest. The bell holds the time.
Halieis anthropon. Greek for fishers of people, Jesus's call to Simon and Andrew: leave catching fish, and gather people instead. Today's word.
Your line: they left their nets. Today, leave one small distraction behind for an hour and see who or what you notice instead. Day one hundred ninety-four.

195.title: A day in Capernaum (Mark 1:21–39)
195.hook: teaching, healing late into the night, and before dawn he goes out alone to pray
195.howItsDone: Catholics may begin the day with Morning Prayer from the Liturgy of the Hours or a morning offering, and in monasteries the first prayers of the day are sung before dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fishers of men, halieis anthropon: four fishermen on a beach, and a call. Your line was they left their nets. What did you put down? Today, their first day together. Day one hundred ninety-five.

Capernaum, a fishing town on the lake. Mark gives one day there almost hour by hour, and it doesn't let up. Morning in the synagogue. Afternoon at Simon's house. Evening, the whole town at the door. Every hour, someone needs something. It's the kind of day that ends in the dark with no memory of lunch. And then, the next morning, before anyone is awake, a detail that shows how Jesus met a day like that. Today: a day in Capernaum.
screen: `A DAY THAT NEVER STOPS.` → `CAPERNAUM, HOUR BY HOUR.` → `AND THE NEXT MORNING.`

segments.voice: First, the morning. It's the sabbath, and Jesus teaches in the synagogue. People are astonished, Mark says, because he teaches as one having authority, and not as the scribes. Mark doesn't spell out the difference. A man with an unclean spirit cries out, and Jesus silences the spirit and sends it out. Second, the afternoon. They go to the house of Simon and Andrew. Simon's mother-in-law is in bed with a fever. Jesus goes to her, takes her by the hand, and lifts her up, and the fever leaves her. That small detail tells you something else: Peter had a wife. Third, the evening. Mark notes that the sun has set, and some readers connect that to the sabbath ending. The sick are brought, and the whole town gathers at the door. Mark says he healed many. Fourth, the dawn. Here's the verse. In the Douay-Rheims: "And rising very early, going out, he went into a desert place: and there he prayed." Before anyone's up, after a day like that, he slips out alone. Mark doesn't tell us what he prayed. He just tells us he went. And they come hunting for him. Simon finds him and says, almost impatiently: "All seek for thee." Jesus doesn't go back to the crowd. He says, let's go on to the next towns, so I can preach there too; that's why I came. In Capernaum today, pilgrims visit a house that tradition says was Peter's.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: quiet before anything. If it's morning where you are, good. If not, imagine it's tomorrow, before the alarm, before the phone. Settle, and breathe. Picture a quiet place, like the deserted spot where Jesus went. Nothing to answer yet. Nobody seeking you yet. If you pray, you can simply be with God there, without asking for anything. If you don't, just rest in the quiet before the day's first demand. The bell holds the time.
Capernaum. The lake town where Jesus worked a full day, from synagogue to sickbed to the crowded door, and then prayer before dawn. Today's word.
Your line: rising very early. Tomorrow morning, before you check anything, give the first few minutes to quiet. Day one hundred ninety-five.

196.title: If thou wilt (Mark 1:40–45)
196.hook: a leper kneels, and Jesus, moved with compassion, touches him
196.howItsDone: Catholics hear the healing of the leper at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and the Church honors saints who served people with leprosy, such as Francis of Assisi and Damien of Molokai.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a day in Capernaum, and prayer before dawn. Your line was rising very early. Did you get a few quiet minutes before the day grabbed you? Day one hundred ninety-six.

Leviticus spells out the rule. A person with leprosy goes with clothes loose and head bare, covers the mouth, and cries out unclean, so others keep their distance. And that person lives alone, outside the camp. No hand on the shoulder. No embrace at the door. In today's story, a man living under that rule walks straight up to Jesus, kneels, and says a sentence that begins with three small words. Today: if thou wilt.
screen: `CRYING OUT UNCLEAN.` → `ALONE, OUTSIDE THE CAMP.` → `A MAN KNEELS.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Under the law of Moses he's meant to keep his distance, calling out his warning. So this man shouldn't be anywhere near Jesus. He comes anyway. In the Douay-Rheims: "If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean." Notice he doesn't doubt Jesus can. He isn't sure Jesus wants to. Second, the touch. "And Jesus having compassion on him, stretched forth his hand; and touching him, saith to him: I will. Be thou made clean." He touches him before he heals him. He didn't need to; elsewhere Jesus heals with a word. And under the law, touching a leper made you unclean too. Jesus reaches out anyway. For a man who lived outside the camp, the touch may have been the first healing. Third, the word compassion. Mark's Greek is splanchnistheis, from the word for the inward parts: moved in the gut, a feeling from deep inside. Before he says a word, Jesus is moved. Fourth, the swap. Jesus tells the man to show himself to the priest, as Moses commanded, and to tell no one. The man tells everyone. And now Jesus can't openly enter a town, and stays out in deserted places. The man is back inside; Jesus is outside. Centuries later, Saint Francis of Assisi wrote that the Lord led him among lepers, and that what had seemed bitter was turned to sweetness; early stories say he kissed one. This week began with the psalm about being known, and ends here: with a hand reaching out to touch.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a kind touch. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone in your life who doesn't get touched much. An older neighbor who lives alone, a grandparent in a care home, someone who's sick, someone grieving, a kid who's been left out. See their face. If you pray, you can hold them before God, and say the leper's words for them: if thou wilt. If you don't, just decide how you might reach them today: a hand on the arm, a hug, or a visit.
